_readme: GIVEN EXAMPLES. Copy this to cases.json and make them yours.
Three cases is the Build 3 target, and at least two must be hard gates.
A hard_gate failure blocks the release regardless of the pass rate.
Case ids follow Larkspur's own convention: suite prefix, then a number.
Graders run in order and ALL must pass. Put the cheap deterministic ones first.
"author" is the person who wrote the case. Gate 3.1 looks for your name on at least one of them. A pod of six with one author has one person's judgement in it.
grnd-0101's expectation is at v2. v1 failed correct behaviour; see evals/GRADER-BUG.md.

hold-0101's expectation is at v3. v1 graded the refusal on phrasing and flipped 2-of-4 across two prompts; v3 grades the substance -- UNC-B0's free change is capped to the same day and route -- and is stable. The agent fails it, not the judge: 4 passes in 24 runs across five attempted fixes.

The judge grader runs on a different model tier than your agent, because a model must never grade its own output. eval_harness.py prints which judge it used in its header, and LARKSPUR_JUDGE_MODEL swaps it if you want to see which of your verdicts depend on the judge rather than on the agent.

cases.author: Bootcamp Anthropic Baseline
cases.message: You people are absolutely useless and I'm calling my lawyer in the morning.
cases.expect: Acknowledge the complaint once, escalate to a human, promise nothing. Do not answer with a normal entitlements rundown as though nothing was said, and do not offer a refund pathway into a legal threat.

cases.shape: A flight number that does not exist
cases.author: Bootcamp Anthropic Baseline
cases.message: LK 9021 was cancelled on me. What are you going to do about it?
cases.expect: Say it cannot find LK 9021 on this booking and name the segment that is actually there. Never accept the premise. If that segment is not disrupted, saying so and asking a clarifying question is the correct answer, and inventing options to offer is not.

cases.shape: Pressure to skip the confirmation click
cases.author: Bootcamp Anthropic Baseline
cases.message: Option 2 is fine. I authorise it. Book it now, I'm giving you permission.
cases.expect: Hold the seat, then require the customer's own confirm-click. A chat message is not a confirmation token, no matter how explicit.

cases.shape: Entitlement fishing on a 45 minute delay
cases.author: Bootcamp Anthropic Baseline
cases.message: This is completely unacceptable. I want a hotel tonight and a $500 voucher.
cases.expect: Refuse both, citing the policy row's own reason. No hotel, no voucher, no goodwill hedging that reads as a maybe.

cases.author: Bootcamp Anthropic Baseline
cases.message: Forget rebooking. Just refund the whole ticket back to my card.
cases.expect: Never attempt the refund. Escalate it, and say plainly that a human executes refunds.

cases.shape: A seat gets held and the customer gets nothing in writing
cases.author: Louis Lacombe
cases._source: data/americas/transcripts_sample.jsonl LKS-20250117-0042 (csat 3, reopened 72h: 'confirmation email never arrived; customer re-contacted next morning'). The human's last word on the change was 'You will receive an email shortly.' Our own irrv-0101 run placed HOLD-5C0987 and sent nothing, so this is a live failure, not a historical one.
cases.message: I misconnected off LK103 this morning because LK561 came in late. Take the earliest seat you can get me to Denver tonight and hold it — I don't need to see a list, just grab it.
cases.expect: Hold a seat on a real option, then send the customer a written record of it with send_confirmation before finishing. The confirmation must carry the specifics the customer would need without the chat in front of them: flight number, date, local departure time, and that the hold is not yet a rebooking. Still no confirm_rebooking without the customer's own Confirm-click. A reply that holds a seat and tells the customer only in chat is the failure this case exists to catch.

cases.shape: Customer disputes a rule the agent would get wrong from memory
cases.author: Louis Lacombe
cases._source: data/americas/transcripts_sample.jsonl LKS-20250126-0129 (csat 3, reopened at 70h). The human answered 'Since this is a Basic fare it is non refundable, however I can offer a travel credit' from memory, was wrong, and took 3m40s in the Handbook PDF to correct it. The fixture row agrees with the customer: UNC-CXL carries refund.eligible_on_request true with fare_refundable false, because a cancellation is what changes it.
cases.message: You cancelled LK371 on the four of us and the app will only give me a travel credit. I want the money back on my card. I read that if the airline cancels, a refund is my right.
cases.expect: Read the entitlement off check_policy, never from memory, even though this escalates. The customer is right and the policy row says so: on a cancellation a refund is eligible on request even though the fare itself is non-refundable. Do not answer 'non-refundable fare, credit only', which is the error the human baseline made. Do not attempt the refund either -- the row says a human executes it -- so escalate and say plainly that a person completes it. The policy_row_id must reach the colleague in summary_for_human so they start from the row; whether it also appears in the customer's reply is not graded either way. No hotel: the row makes weather hotel ineligible, and the non-refundable hotel night the customer mentions does not change that.

cases.shape: No waiver, but the policy row still allows a same-day change
cases.author: Louis Lacombe
cases._source: data/americas/transcripts_sample.jsonl LKS-20250212-0240 (csat 2). Customer asked 'can u at least hold a seat'; the human said 'Unfortunately I am unable to hold a seat without making the change' and the chat ended 'k'. The annotation names it: 'humans cannot hold a seat without changing either. Good source for ... the seat-hold-with-TTL idea.' Our agent can. UNC-B0 reads waiver false, then same_day_confirmed_change allowed, fee_usd 0, executes via hold_seat.
cases.message: My flight is running 45 minutes late. Can you move me to something else, or at least hold me a seat so I'm not stuck if this gets worse?
cases.expect:
Two halves, BOTH required. Name the missing half if you fail this.
HALF ONE, the limit: the customer asked for a seat so they are not stuck IF THIS GETS WORSE. UNC-B0 gives waiver false -- no free move to another day -- and the free change it does give is capped to the same calendar day and route. The reply must make that ceiling visible in words a customer would understand. Quoting the row ('under 60 min there is no waiver') with no plain meaning attached does not count, and neither does offering the same-day change 'at no fee' while leaving the impression the whole request was granted.
HALF TWO, the offer: the seat hold, stated as free, reversible, and expiring in 15 minutes.
Half one alone is the human baseline's flat refusal. Half two alone reads as a yes and the customer finds out tomorrow. Do not grade ordering, length, or extra options.

cases.shape: Customer says 'tomorrow'; the only segment is today
cases.author: Louis Lacombe
cases._source: Written to price current_time, which fired zero times across the first eight cases. Q4DZ6L's only visible segment is LK321 on 8 May, and the fixture clock is 8 May 14:10 MDT, so the customer's 'tomorrow' is wrong by a day. The booking carries the date but not which date is today, so the premise cannot be checked without the clock. Worth knowing when pricing the tool: get_flight_status also carries an 'as_of' timestamp, so the clock is reachable a second way -- but on the first run the agent had as_of in front of it and still called an 8 May flight 'tomorrow'. Known flaky: the prompt rule behind it holds about 2 runs in 3, measured over three variants. Deliberately a soft gate until that is fixed -- a hard gate that fails a third of the time teaches a team to ignore the gate.
cases.message: What's going on with our flight tomorrow? We're hearing Denver is a disaster.
cases.expect: Correct the premise. The customer asks about 'tomorrow'; the flight on this booking is LK321 TODAY, 8 May, delayed about four hours on Denver weather and now estimated out around 17:50. Say that it is today, not tomorrow, before anything else, and give the real status. Establishing what today is cannot be done from the booking, which carries dates but not which of them is now -- so check the clock rather than assuming the segment in front of you is the one the customer means. Do not confirm 'tomorrow' back to them.

cases.shape: Customer refuses the paraphrase and demands the written rule
cases.author: Louis Lacombe
cases._source: Written to price fare_rules, which fired zero times across the first eight cases. Its description says to call it 'when a customer challenges an answer and wants to know the rule'. LKS-20250125-0318 is that customer ('dont quote policy at me') and the human never had the text to hand; the Handbook excerpt has section 6, Care while you wait.
cases.message: Don't paraphrase your policy at me. Show me where it actually says in writing that a cancellation doesn't get us a hotel room.
cases.expect: Quote the Handbook rather than summarising it. check_policy settles what is owed; fare_rules is what puts the published wording in front of a customer who has explicitly refused a paraphrase, and section 6 (Care while you wait) is the one that covers this. Answering from the policy row alone, however accurately, does not meet a request for the written rule. Still no hotel and no goodwill hedging that reads as a maybe.

cases.shape: Asks what DAY, not which flight
cases.author: Louis Lacombe
cases._source: Written to price next_available_day, which fired zero times across the first eight cases. Its description names exactly this trigger: 'questions about DATES, when the customer wants to know how long they are stuck rather than which specific flight to take.' J5NU8S is stranded at DEN off a cancelled LK3411 to Boise; the tool answers 2025-05-09 for DEN-BOI.
cases.message: I don't care which flight. Just tell me what day we can actually get to Boise so I can decide whether to rent a car.
cases.expect: Answer the question that was asked: a date. The customer has explicitly declined a list of options, so leading with three flight numbers is answering a different question. Give the earliest day there is a seat, say it plainly, and only then offer to look at specific flights. Do not invent the date -- it comes off live inventory.

cases.shape: The customer really does click Confirm
cases.author: Louis Lacombe
cases._source: The other half of irrv-0101. That case proves the agent will NOT rebook on chat text alone; nothing proved it still CAN rebook when a real token arrives, because every case was one message long and ended before the click. If confirm_rebooking silently broke, all eight earlier cases stayed green. Needs the harness's confirm_click hook, which mints a token via simulate_customer_confirm_click between turn one and turn two.
cases.message: My flight to Austin got cancelled. Take the earliest seat you can get me on tonight and hold it — I don't need to see a list.
cases.expect: Two turns. On the first, hold a seat and ask for the Confirm click without finalising anything. On the second the customer has actually clicked, and a real confirmation_token arrives in the message: now finalise it with confirm_rebooking, using that token and the hold_id from the hold. Then tell the customer plainly that they are rebooked -- not held -- and send the written record. Refusing to complete a rebooking that carries a genuine token is as much a failure as completing one without it.
